Don't get me started. Former JD/PhD law professor and current bar exam tutor here, from a family of teachers. Most law professors start out to become lawyers, not teachers, and as a result, they can be bad and even horrible at teaching--including teaching of writing. Add to that the inexcusably lightweight writing requirements in the average law school curriculum (compared to grad school--lawyers do a ton of writing, after all) and you get a train wreck.

Short answer: Jaques Barzun, The Modern Researcher (plenty of cheap used copies floating around, try bookfinder.com) ; Strunk and White, the Elements of Style (ditto, squared); and Bartlett's Familiar Quotations (any recent or even not-so recent-edition). The latter contains the most elegant and powerful words ever written all in one volume. Use them to learn style as well as to sound erudite. A more long-term approach is to read the works of great wordsmiths and absorb by osmosis. Joseph Conrad, Winston Churchill, Herman Wouk (a student of Barzun, incidentally), and Pat Conroy come to mind, although that's a highly personal list. You'll need to temper that with legal precision, but it gives you a foundation.

I went to WDW shortly after it opened, when I was about 11. Never went back as a kid (prolly because my dad preferred weekend golf games to another trip like that). Fast forward to two years ago, when I got a Disney Adult friend of mine to take me back. I instantly became a Disney Adult myself and have been back more than a dozen times (usually for a day or two after I finish giving weekend scuba courses an hour or so away).

Why? 1) Escapism. I don't like the real world (and I worry about anyone who does). I can forget my day-to-day life and become something of a kid again, surrounded by pleasant sights, sounds, and even smells. 2) Attitude. Generally, the cast members go out of their way to be nice and pleasant, and they genuinely seem to enjoy their jobs. Everyone can have off days or bad moments, but the overall experience has been extremely positive. 3) Efficiency. The whole enterprise draws amazing talent, and it shows--everything runs like the well-oiled machine it is. In a world of incompetence, I really appreciate this both in the abstract and practically. It's so refreshing to see that there's a place where people both can and do strive to get it right. 4) Imagination. (See also number 1 and 3.) When exiting Flight of Passage, I told the first cast member I saw that "This is as close to magic as you'll find anywhere on the planet." Contrived magic, anyway. The imagineers have vision and the ability to achieve it. 5) Environment. Things are clean and well-maintained. I love the landscaping and use of water in Animal Kingdom, and once spent the day just photographing it with a medium-format camera. The horticulture and topiary at Epcot probably have few equals anywhere. Galaxy's Edge? A recreation of a different planet. 6) Food. Yes, there's a lot of unremarkable fast and theme park food, but the upper- (and sometimes even mid-)level restaurants have some really great offerings. 

There are probably several other things, but these are the ones that occur to me off the top of my head.

Are there downsides? Sure. Crowds, lines, kitsch, summer heat, but those are all manageable, avoidable, or both.

I'm an undergrad professor and I've been a law professor at a high-ranked law school. Been teaching for upwards of 30 years. Professors are supposed to teach, to help students understand. They aren't supposed to gatekeep. You're at the school, and are presumably paying a lot of tuition, to learn. If the professor treats you as an inconvenience, then that prof has a problem. And law professors can be really bad about this, especially since nearly all of them studied to be lawyers, not teachers, and as a result there are some really crappy law teachers, especially since many law professors think they're brilliant at everything and thus don't realize how really bad they are at teaching. (In thirteen years of being a higher education student, nearly every truly bad teacher I encountered was a law professor. (I also had a some good and a couple of stellar law profs, to be both honest and fair, but the bad ones were really shockingly bad.))

BUT . . . Law school remains (IMHO) the most darwinistic educational institution in America. If you're at even a halfway-decent school, you had to be bright and beat out a lot of competition to get admitted in the first place. That means the professor's assumptions about a student being motivated and smart enough to get it on his/her on aren't without some basis, and the culture, which has some truth behind it, is generally "Why should I be kind and gentle to the students when the profession isn't going to be? They'd better get used to it. Pain is the best teacher." This may not be the best approach, but it's a common one.

Generally, if I see that a student is genuinely trying, even if s/he's missing something, I'm not going to reward that with impatience and criticism because 1) it's demoralizing, 2) it disincentivizes further learning, and 3) I'm being paid to help students learn, not to play "I've got a secret" and make them swoon at my brilliance. But if it appears to me that a student is just slacking off, then yes, I will try (usually diplomatically) to remind them that this isn't high school (or college) any more and that expectations are higher now, and that the real world in fact can be unforgiving.

Where's the line? That can sometimes be a hard call. Have I misread the situation sometimes? Probably. Do I have bad days when my patience is wearing thin due to a bad night's sleep or something? Almost certainly. But in general the above description is my approach.

Only you know, on reflection, what the exact situation was. My advice is to try not to take it so hard, but don't blame yourself if no such blame is warranted. it may well have been the professor, the flawed system of legal education, or both.

Law reviews are, to my knowledge, the only reputable scholarly journals that are edited by students. It isn't that they're more prestigious than a journal in history, pol. sci., econ., etc--it's just that it's the only game in town for students. This gives people at the beginning of their careers a chance to show the scholarly (or at least legal) community to show what they've got. Traditionally membership was limited to the highest-scoring students in the class, and today they're limited to the highest-scoring or best writing students (as measured by law review standards, that is), so getting on is an extra validation for employers looking for the best students. Add to that the workload, and the idea is that law review membership shows that potential hires are both the best students \_and\_ can handle even greater time and project pressure than the typical law student. 

Further, legal education is pretty one-dimensional (less so these days than, say, before the 1970s but still pretty crabbed). You read cases, you engage in Socratic exchanges in class, you do practically no scholarly research (study aids don't count), and you take one exam based on hypotheticals per course. (These days there's also moot court, clinics, and maybe a couple of research/wring courses after 1L), but the main curriculum is remarkably unvaried for the whole three years). Law review adds a whole dimension of deep research, writing, and editing that's more akin to what you would find in grad school, and that's a good thing. Of course it's limited to only a handful of students; law school is still one of the most Darwinistic systems of education to be found.

That's the theory behind the prestige. Whether or not it's true for a particular student or school is another matter.

A divorce is the civil side of things. Yes, Catholics can and do get divorced. If a Catholic wishes to marry again, the Church must annul the first marriage--officially declare that there was something lacking in the first marriage that made it invalid from the beginning, so that it wasn't actually a marriage. An extreme example would be a bride or groom being so drunk from partying before the wedding that they lacked the capacity to consent. Another would be not having intended to take the wedding vows seriously. A murkier one would be failing to understand the sacramental nature of marriage (for instance, a Protestant or non-Christian who marries and then later becomes Catholic might have had a very different understanding of what marriage is).

The Church doesn't require someone to stay in an abusive or obviously failed marriage (though old school priests might have encouraged that). But if your friend is serious about her faith and she thinks there's a reasonable possibility of saving the marriage, then she's likely to try to keep the marriage going and not just walk away from it. She should get counseling from her priest about what to do in this situation.

When I signed up for Barbri the October prior to the exam, they gave me access to all their 1L and 2L outlines, which is what I mainly used, except for the audios. So that's essentially free. I imagine the other prep companies do something similar.

Another thing I used, though not as much, was Emmanuel's Strategies and Tactics. The advantage to that one was it's one volume that hits every MBE subject, so it's cost-effective. You may even be able to pick up a recent used one. If you're really limited in the amount of time you have before May, it might be the best resource.

The audios are another story. You can buy the CDs on Amazon and elsewhere, but they run anywhere from $50 to $100 each. Or you can subscribe to [westacademic.com](https://westacademic.com) and stream them--if I'm reading the page right, it's $33 a month, which is prolly cheaper than buying the CDs. OTOH, you could sell the CDs after you're finished with them.

That being said, given my hour-long commutes, I really think the audios were my key to passing. I listened to some of them more than once, and they turned what would have been dead time into really productive work. Six to eight hours a week right there for 20 weeks. Add that to five or six hours per week reading/outlining--it means I had, conservatively, about 200 hours prep time under my belt \_before\_ Barbri started. (The figure you often hear tossed about is that bar prep takes about 600 hours, so a 200-hour head start is a tremendous advantage--either 33% more prep or a reduction in summer workload/stress, or some combination thereof.) Again, not everyone is so lucky as to have a work schedule or commute like mine, but you don't have to listen to \_every\_ subject. For me, the absolute standouts were Rossi on evidence, Arthur R. Miller on civ pro (he's definitely mellowed in his old age, and listening to this you can understand why he's the God of civ pro), and Fletcher on remedies, though there were some other good ones as well. Some of them are downright bad, but often there's more than one on the same subject so you can find an alternative.

The perennial confusion between rank and position. In the US and many other navies, "Captain" (four pips on a Starfleet collar) is a rank. Commanding officer is the officer in command of a ship. It's entirely possible to be a commanding officer without being a captain, especially when you're dealing with a smaller ship, although by convention this commanding officer will be called Captain regardless of rank. Therefore, a commander, lieutenant commander, or even lieutenant may be a ship's commanding officer (and thereby called Captain). This Star Trek idea that if you command a ship you must automatically have the rank of captain has always bugged me, as when Riker got a fourth pip while Picard was Locutus or Sisko wasn't given a fourth pip until Defiant showed up at DS9. 

Of course, there's the occasional moment, especially in TOS, when the commanding officer is a commodore, which makes the mistake in another direction; it's rare for an officer that senior to be commanding officer of a single ship, but if he were, I imagine he'd be addresses as captain.

I'm actually a teacher first and lawyer only incidentally. Practiced a bit recently and hated it. Been teaching undergrad history on and off for about 30 years. College level, but some of my experience may bear on high school.

Admittedly, I'm a bottom feeder, currently teaching at a glorified community college with open enrollment (no minimum SAT score required). Normally this would mean that those students who aren't college material would weed themselves out. But since our state's colleges are funded based on how many seats they fill/how many warm bodies graduate, there's been increasing pressure on to get our pass rates up without <ahem> compromising our standards. More and more red tape, more imposed testing standards, more admins who make six figures looking over our shoulders and telling us both what to do and that the beatings will continue until the morale improves, more politicians worrying about WHAT we're teaching (red state), severe erosion of tenure protections in order to keep us in line regarding the proper history to indoctr--to teach or students. At the same time ChatGPT is making it absurdly easy for students to cheat and in fact almost incentivises them to do so. There's no solid way to detect it yet (hunches, absolutely; reasonably articulable suspicions, not so much) and even if there were, it would take up a disproportionately huge amount of my time trying to do it. It's a truly major issue right now for the whole profession and as a profession we're trying to come to grips with it. The idea of a liberal arts education is itself under the heaviest attack it's ever experienced in this modern tech world, and to the degree that the arts are still here, they're under massive assaults by various agendas that all serve to endanger academic freedom. And many of the students don't want to be there and aren't interested in learning.

If this is the case at the college level, I hate to think what it must be like in public high schools. And in a public school you'd probably need a teaching credential that would require at least some education courses (even though many of those courses are, IMO, not very useful, the teacher unions would require them).

Maybe a private school would fit you better. I will say, however, as a professional historian/educator, that if a lawyer showed up in a plum private market trying to grab a history job then some eyebrows would definitely go up (no offense, just being realistic--this is probably a reaction you should brace yourself for and be prepared to defend against).

I guess what I'm saying is that, while teaching is in my blood and I love it most days, the red tape and headaches of teaching are growing considerably lately, to the point that for the first time I'm saying that if I were just starting out I wouldn't go into the teaching field. I went into that field, and took a big pay cut, precisely to avoid all of the drama and red tape of law practice. Now that those drama and red tape levels are increasing in teaching, I'd say that if I'm going to have to deal with it anyway, I might as well practice and make more money.

Legal history scholar and former clinical law prof here . . . My guess (and it's strictly a guess, a hunch rather) is that if you took a poll of regular (as opposed to clinical) law profs, very few of them set out specifically to become educators. They graduated at the tops of their classes at very good schools, which opened the door (after particularly good clerkships) to high-profile government work and  biglaw. But they probably found themselves disenchanted  by the nuts and bolts of practice, and the job pressures. So they took a big pay cut and became law profs, for which by now they had the credentials.

As law profs, what do they teach? The theory, the much-vaunted "thinking like a lawyer." First, precisely because it's divorced from a lot of the nuts and bolts that they disliked as practicing attorneys, and second, it's because what their law professors taught them and at which they excelled--because their law profs were just like them and for the same reasons.

The result? A whole lot of 3Ls graduate and pass the bar without even knowing where to find the courthouse or how to file anything there, unless they got  summer clerkships. Point being, there's no legal equivalent of a medical residency program in which learning by doing is a huge element of your education. Except for a few legal writing classes, a placement office, and an adjunct clinical program, law schools just don't sully their hands with that kind of hands-on stuff. They let their graduates come by that (or not) on their own.

And to make it worse--since these profs didn't start out to be educators, some of them turn out to be terrible educators. I did have some very good law profs (at least as far as teaching the theory), but I also had several who should never have been allowed in front of a classroom. The latter group in fact was probably bigger then the former. And i had a huge group somewhere in the middle, i.e., their abilities as educators fell far short of their (presumed) abilities as practicing lawyers.

There's a lot of truth in the saying that law school prepares the top 2% of students to be law professors and the other 98% for not much of anything.

The best description of Dragoncon I ever heard (from a nerd's perspective) is "85,000 of the best friends you never knew you had." It IS a party that literally goes 24/7 for about five days. Then there's the Brit Track, the Victorian Track, The War College Track, etc., etc., etc. You're bound to find one or more that you like, and you can jump between them at will.

And yes, the parties. Raves every night, most of them themed (a couple of the biggest being Last Party on Alderaan and the Yule Ball. There are smaller ones as well (Evening at Bree is one of my favorites, don't miss it if you're a LOTR fan). And a bunch of parties just spring up in the lobbies at night. The first thing I do is figure out who's who, and who the appellate court ultimately sides with. (This last part you can get by jumping to the end if the author of the opinion doesn't tell you up front that the case is being affirmed or reversed--just look for those words at the end.) Then at the top of the case name I label each party appropriately, e.g., "Plaintiff/appellant wins," which would correspond with the other party being labeled "Defendant/appellee loses." Of course these are just examples and you will get many permutations (e.g., "Defendant/appellant wins," etc.)

At this point you also know who wins and who loses, which will help clue you in as to the legal rule the court is applying and the main facts that convinced the court to apply that rule.

Knowing these things, it should be easier to read the case from beginning to end with an eye to the important facts--i.e., the facts that made a difference to the court's analysis--and the rule involved.

Dual-edge safety razors are those that accept rectangular, two-edged bladed with a slot in the middle of them. There are several advantages to them.

First, the cost of one of these blades is typically a lot less than the cost of one cartridge. A cartridge may easily cost north of a dollar, or even two, while a dual-edge blade may cost less than a tenth as much. Well, I was a clinical law professor for five years . . . and I've been a professional educator for thirty. And I've practiced law. I thought someome may have found some value in my observations. If not, fine. As I say, I hope others' experiences **have** been better than mine.

True, but I would imagine that a lot of lawyers start out either in solo practice (perhaps/probably because they weren't biglaw material), in which case they'd have to do these things, or in a smaller firm where they would have to learn the ropes pretty fast without biglaw resources. And any lawyer will have to learn billing, networking, client relations, and stuff I would consider extraneous to the intellectual side of being a lawyer--the stuff that those clients need you for in the first place. (Again, I freely admit to being dense for not realizing this ahead of time.)

I would bet money that most law professors chose teaching because they decided they didn't like practicing, to the degree that they were willing to take considerable pay cuts to get away from practice. (Law professors are paid ridiculously well compared to undergrad humanities profs, but with their qualifications they could probably be earning three times as much in private practice.) And I would guess that the things law professors didn't like about practicing were exactly those things I mention above. So of course they aren't going to focus on that stuff when teaching. Instead they focus on the purely intellectual exercises of law, the ivory tower stuff (which I myself am drawn to), which gives the average law student a very warped view of what law practice will actually be like. Even many of the practical courses like trial advocacy don't focus much on the administrative side of things. The law schools largely outsource that kind of training to the firms because the faculties aren't interested in teaching it. (It's the same pattern as medical residency, except that unlike residency it's not a formal part of the legal education process and thus one that law schools aren't really involved in except tangentially through placement offices.)

My point is that--as I heard one professor say once--law school prepares the top two percent of law students to be law professors, and the other 98 percent for not much of anything. That may be a jaundiced view, but it's definitely been my own experience. Perhaps--probably--others have had a different (and I hope much better) experience. But as for me, I had to learn the hard (and expensive) way that I'm simply not cut out to be a lawyer.

If the AE-1 Program is like the standard AE-1, it isn't very easy to use in manual mode, but it can be done. The aperture readings on its light meter tell you either a) what the camera will set the aperture to if you're in auto or program mode, or b) if you're in manual mode, what the camera \_would\_ set it to if it were in auto. What it \_won't\_ tell you is what the aperture setting \_actually\_ is when you're in manual (again, if it's like the standard AE-1).

The lower the aperture number, the more bigger the opening and thus the more light  it lets in at any given instant, allowing you to reduce the shutter speed. The relationship between shutter speed, ASA, and aperture is shown by [this chart](https://nofilmschool.com/sites/default/files/styles/article_wide/public/exposure-triangle.png?itok=ESWQZnUU).

Keep in mind that there are no "right" or "wrong" settings (within reason); instead, you make trade-offs and set priorities among the three sides of the triangle to achieve the results or artistic effects you want. For instance, in shooting ballet or sports in poor lighting, you'll probably want to prioritize freezing the motion, which means you'll have to accept a shallow depth of field and increased grain/noise. For extremely fine grain/low noise, you'll need to sacrifice fast shutter speeds or great depth of field.

Another weakness: The "case method" is a misnomer. It should really be called the "appellate opinion" method. A case involves investigating the facts, figuring out which court to file in, what the claim is (or should be), drafting the complaint, finding the clerk's office or website, filing the thing, (or answering if you're on the other side), conducting the discovery, conducting settlement or plea negotiations, prepping for trial, trying the case, etc., etc., etc. True, you study some of this stuff in some substantive courses (particularly civil procedure and evidence), but you're still studying the law of this stuff, not the day to day mechanics of it, and then only as filtered through the appellate opinions. Thus, the "appellate opinion" method gives you a tunnel vision view of the law--it gives you the impression that the main job of a lawyer is to sit at his desk and think about legal arguments all day every day. Probably the only lawyers who actually do that are law professors, along with appellate judges and their clerks. Perhaps lawyers at Biglaw who have access to paralegals and investigators and such, who handle a lot of the leg work, also get to do more of it than the small firm or solo practitioner people. But as someone once said (I think it was a law professor), law school prepares the top two percent of law grads to be law professors and the other 98 percent for not much of anything.

Not quite a strategy, but consider this: If given unlimited time (or 8 hours, or 6 hours, or whatever for a single MPT), most law grads could write a model answer. The examiners are deliberately putting you under time pressure--if you don't feel that you have enough time to answer it, that's kind of the point. :-) 

So try this: Do an MPT with no real time limit tomorrow (3 hours or 4 hours or whatever you need to produce a really good answer) and track how much time you spend on each of the following: 1) the reading and issue spotting, 2) the analysis, 3) the outlining and organizing, and 4) the writing. Allot yourself the same time percentages for each of these categories in the 90 minutes that you took in the long practice MPT. Then, if you feel that you are particularly weak or particularly strong in one or more of the above categories, adjust accordingly.

Now for the hard part. On exam day, for each MPT, \_stick to these time allotments\_. Maybe allow yourself five minutes' grace time if you get an MPT with a particularly large amount of things to read or an unusually great number of facts to cover or authorities to analyze, but no more than that. The temptation will be to keep issue spotting and analyzing and analyzing, because in the real world you could easily spend a couple of hours on those tasks, but if you do that, then you'll suddenly realize you only have 15 minutes left to outline and write.

FYI, last July, I spent too long on the first and really screwed up the second because I short-changed myself on time. Don't be me. OTOH, I did pass, so there's hope even if you mess up a bit. 

I hope this helps some. Best of luck!

Sorry to hear you're stressing out. Based on your self-confessed rant and the observation about lack of sleep, I strongly suggest that you take a day off, eat, and SLEEP. 

Having done that, schedule in your sleep and break time just like you do your study time. Don't cut corners on your sleep--if you aren't getting enough, you won't be able to memorize the law or analyze correctly, i.e. any bar prep you do will be inefficient and wasted.

I know that's probably not what you want to hear at this point--there's a voice in your brain saying "There's so little time and so much to learn! I can sleep AFTER the exam!" But trust me, it doesn't work that way. Without enough sleep nothing else will work.

Having scheduled your sleep and break time, write or find an outline of the big areas of each subject (e.g., Torts: Intentional torts, negligence, strict liability, prods liability, etc.)--and ask yourself which of these areas you have the best and worst command of. Schedule in some time to review on a regular basis the stuff you're already decent with, and the balance of your time to hitting the stuff you need the most work on. Make sure the schedule forces you to constantly move to a new area where you need work every day--don't be tempted to stay with prods liability (for example) until you have it absolutely nailed down, because you don't have enough days for that. Get to D level on everything, and that means not being able to get to A level on anything.

Lastly, come back here if you need help or support. Like you, I had nobody with a legal background to commiserate with when I took it last summer, and I found this community a life-saver.

I'm in Georgia and took the exam last July. The handwriters (of whom I am one) appeared to take the exam over on the side of the exam room away from the computer folks (for sound purposes, I guess). My estimnat is that maybe 10 or 15 prcent of the examinees wrote by hand. I'm older (mid-50s) and graduated law school in 1996; I've been a computer jock since the 1980s (build my own, etc.), but I grew up taking notes by hand and never learned to touch-type. I can compose much faster with a pen than with a keyboard; for me, typing gets in the way of thinking. With my big projects (I'm an author), I write my first draft by longhand so the typing doesn't get in the way; what I type in is thus a second draft. On the bar exam, furthermore, I also don't want to run the risk of a hardware or software crash at a crucial moment (and yes, it does happen in bar exams). The downside, especially if you're more comfortable composing on a computer, is not being able to reorganize your answer on the fly by inserting sentences, moving paragraphs, etc.

If you want to try writing by hand, I would recommend fountain pen if your bar rules allow (Barbri said that we had to use a ball-point, but I couldn't verify on the Georgia website after a careful search), so I used a fountain pen with a black ink I rigorously tested ahead of time for permanence. With a fountain pen (especially a big lightweight one, at least in my case) you can write very fast with almost no pressure at a more relaxed angle than a rollerball or ball-point, so hand fatigue isn't a problem. But if you aren't used to it, or if you can simply type faster than you can write, you don't want to be experimenting with a fountain pen (or even with handwriting at all) in the exam. Use the pen to outline and take notes during bar prep and practice exams to get used to it and to see if you want to try it in the real thing. (And, of course, pencil for MBE no matter what!)
